Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. Du Bois spoke about being black in America as having a “double-consciousness,” and I can say growing up as the black American child of Eritrean immigrants that I felt a triple-consciousness. There can be extreme trauma and difficulty in growing up and living in America as a first-generation black person: from Eritrean cultural dislocation to coming to terms with a white supremacist history of exploitation. The fact that many of our parents don’t have language or awareness to help us navigate the problems of race and racism here can exacerbate our struggle. But there is also a blessing that comes from being racialized into marginalization: the opportunity and necessity for radical empathy. Even if they were not all directly my histories, I felt the pain of slavery, segregation, racism, genocide, and colonialism in me

[PDF page 2] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses as a black person. I knew how hypocritical it would be for me to, even latently, support any system of oppression, when I understood the feeling of being oppressed myself. I certainly don’t believe blackness or a group’s history of marginalization is a prerequisite for radical empathy, but, for me, this understanding helped me unpack my own privilege at a young age, helped me stand in solidarity with other oppressed groups, and helped serve as a foundation for my own activism and work in education. It bestowed upon me a liberatory politics that critiqued and questioned a status quo built on and sustained by imperialism, racism, heteropatriarchy, and economic exploitation, and affirmed that the artifice of stability should never preclude people’s right to freedom, equality, and justice. I became aware of the LGBT civil rights movement after the brutal murder of Matthew Shephard. As a young teenager, I became aware of the ways homophobic language was normalized in the communities I grew up in, and I challenged it anywhere I heard it. When I became a teacher, I ensured LGBTQ+ histories were included in my curriculum, and I helped create accountable interventions with social workers around transphobic and homophobic bullying. An understanding of universal human rights and indivisible justice for all were at the center of my curriculum and discipline protocol, which afforded a frame for respecting and acknowledging difference, developing tolerance, and building empathy. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? I am a first-generation American, a product of Eritrean immigrants, a brother, a proud Mount Vernon resident, a special education teacher, a Knicks fan. As a child, I internalized my parents’ revolutionary efforts in support of Eritrean liberation and connected it to the struggles for recognition and inclusion in the worlds I knew. Growing up in Mount Vernon, I was exposed to inequality around all me. The contradictions apparent in the different communities I was steeped in provoked a justice-seeking politics within me and has informed my professional career. I graduated from Yale with degrees in Political Science and Economics and then CCNY with a Master’s in Secondary Special Education. I became a special education teacher largely because of the inequities I saw in different school systems growing up. I have now been in education for over 10 years (in the Bronx, Washington Heights, and Palestine). School can be a site of liberation and discovery, but, for most of my students, school put them in the pipeline to prison instead of a path to college. I am proud that – in my classroom – I was able to provide a safe space for my students to holistically develop their intelligences, while giving them the critical tools to question not only what they learn but their position in society.

[PDF page 3] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses As teachers, we not only manage 35 teenagers in underfunded classrooms daily, we get our young people to believe in themselves when the world has told them they shouldn’t. Teaching special education in NYC, I had to demystify education for many of my students, some who entered my 8th grade class on a 1st grade reading level. They’ve been failed every step of the way, so when they arrive in my class, my job is to create a plan in concert with them and a host of diverse stakeholders in the community - social workers, parents, coaches, religious leaders – to ensure they progress. Collaborating to implement needed interventions is exactly what I will be doing in Congress for communities that have been underserved and neglected for too long and for a country that has as little faith in government as my students did in school. Why I’m Running? I am running for office because the district I have known my whole life is not best served by a militaristic Democrat like Eliot Engel. I taught in my district in an underfunded, segregated school, where my 12-year olds walked through metal detectors at 7:45 AM into a school that had 1 social worker for 500 students. It became irreconcilable to me that this was our unabating reality while our public money was being diverted to unnecessary wars. Our community is more concerned with investments in education, health care, housing, and jobs than wasteful military spending. We are focusing on fighting climate change and securing a Global Green New Deal, but that’s only possible if we divest from the military industrial complex and pursue the multilateralism necessary to have the world aligned on shared climate goals. Engel has been in Congress for 30 years, rising to the Chair of House Foreign Affairs, and he's been one of the leading Democratic proponents of an immoral foreign policy our district is against: voting for the Iraq War, opposing Obama’s Iran deal, stonewalling action against Saudi Arabia in Yemen, and challenging efforts to hold the Israeli government accountable. I am running because, as my students’ families are struggling here, and our cousins are dying in US-wars abroad, these hawkish Democrats can no longer represent us. The imperialist militarization of US foreign policy weakens democracy at home. Fighting the entrenchment of the police state, deportation apparatus, and mass surveillance, as well as increasing white nationalism, necessitates championing a progressive foreign policy. Such a foreign policy vision provides the moral foundation and fiscal flexibility to advocate for social programs that deepen our democracy, secure working people’s freedom, and guarantee rights/justice for historically marginalized groups. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. The LGBTQ+ community has historically been disproportionately affected by housing and workplace discrimination, but, in this era of Trump, anti-LGBTQ+ violence is rapidly

In 2018, for example, at least 26 trans people were murdered, the majority of whom were black women. We demand an end to the violence, and we will continue to fight for full equality for all LGTBQ+ people. Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. I have supported the rights of the LGBTQ+ community throughout my time in office. I am currently a co-sponsor on the Equality Act, a comprehensive civil rights bill which would offer protection against discrimination for LGBTQ+ people. Last week, my advocacy to free Chin Mei Tsui from ICE custody succeeded when Gov. Cuomo granted Chin a pardon, and ICE subsequently released him. I am currently working to ensure that every family in the country has access to paid family leave, building on my work to include LGBTQ+ families in these policies both in Congress and, previous to that, as a member of the NYC city council.

[PDF page 11] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses I have a long history of supporting LGBTQ+ rights, including work on marriage equality, ending Don't Ask Don't Tell, adoption access, education, employment, and international LGBTQ+ rights. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? I have served in Congress since 1993, and over that time have achieved a number of things for NY-12 and NYC. Most recently, that includes passing the 9/11 Victims Compensation Fund, obtaining funding for major public infrastructure projects, including L-train repairs and the Kosciuszko Bridge, fighting for the Equal Rights Amendment, passing consumer protection measures for corporate board diversity and ending unfair banking practices, and finding ways to address our district and country's growing inequality. Having represented the community throughout my career, I have a firm understanding of the issues that matter in NY-12 - and have the experience and knowledge of how to work within the system to address those issues. Having built a publicly-funded health care system with the 9/11 programs, I know we can fight for and win Medicare for All while protecting the ACA - and the 135 million Americans who depend on it - from GOP sabotage. As a lifelong advocate for the environment, I fought to get Newtown Creek declared a superfund site and have pushed for better environmental standards and corporate responsibility towards the environment - and now I am an original co-sponsor on the Green New Deal, because we must address the climate crisis NOW. I have fought for NYCHA and affordable housing, and am a co-sponsor on the Green New Deal for Public Housing. Last year, I became the first woman elected to chair the House Committee on Oversight and Reform, and that has enabled me to shine a national spotlight on some of our most pressing issues. One of my first actions was to impeach Donald Trump, and I've kept up the pressure on his administration since then with demands for financial documents and other records that would show the extent of his corruption. In addition, I've already held hearings on inclusive, universal paid family leave, on the ways in which the Trump administration is using religion to discriminate against LGBTQ+ Americans, on states' draconian laws opposing abortion access, on the cruel border policies this administration has enacted, and most recently, a two-day hearing on the administration's lackluster response to the Coronavirus, among other topics. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. Last year, we passed the Equality Act in the Senate - we will continue to work to pass this bill and safeguard these vital protections for our LGBTQ+ friends and neighbors. I am also working to ensure the Trump administration cannot misuse "religious exemptions" to create a license to discriminate against LGBTQ+ people. I also recently

Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. As a member of the House Equality Caucus, I am a staunch defender of the LGBTQ community. I believe that LGBTQ equality is one of the defining civil rights issues of our time, and we’ve endured many years of legal and social struggle to guarantee today’s recognition of the love and commitment of our LGBTQ friends, family, and neighbors. Unfortunately, too many in the LGBTQ community still face discrimination and are denied the full equality they deserve. That is why I was proud to cosponsor and vote for H.R. 5, the Equality Act,

[PDF page 18] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses earlier this year. When it came before the House, I gave a 1-minute speech urging my colleagues to support this critical legislation. I will continue to fight for the dignity and equal rights of all LGBTQ Americans. I am proud to have been endorsed by the Stonewall Democrats of New York City in last election cycle. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? From my first years in Congress, I have fought to protect the rights of LGBTQ Americans. I was one of the few House Members who voted against the Defense of Marriage Act in 1996. Thankfully, the Supreme Court eventually struck it down, but I voted against it in 1996 because it was the right thing to do. I voted against it because I believe every man and woman deserves the right to love whomever they choose, without fear of discrimination from their government. I voted against it because I know those who stand against equality stand on the wrong side of history. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. Throughout my career in Congress I have led efforts nationally and internationally to advance the rights of LGBTQ people. Every year I introduce a resolution supporting the Day of Silence to bring attention to anti-LGBTQ bullying and harassment and encourage schools to adopt anti-discrimination policies. As Chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, I have also introduced, cosponsored and advanced bills and resolutions on human rights in the Foreign Affairs Committee and in the full House of Representatives. These measures address the human rights situations for the Uyghurs, Tibetans, Rohingya, Central Americans, the humanitarian crisis in Syria, Yemen, South Sudan, Democratic Republic of Congo and Venezuela, human trafficking victims, LGBTQ individuals, among others. I will continue to advance the cause of human rights in our foreign policy and call out the Administration when they are lacking in leadership on these issues. Please explain any activities and/or experiences that demonstrate your commitment to the LGBT civil rights movement. I have worked with the Alliance for Quality Education and members of the state assembly and state senate to push the Safe and Supportive Schools act forward. This piece of legislation ensures that schools are adequately resourced with guidance counselors and social workers to ensure that every school is a safe haven for kids regardless of background or orientation or identity. My work with AQE and others seeks to ensure that our schools are trauma informed and effective at implementing restorative justice practices. As many LGBTQ youth are victims of bullying, these measures will directly impact how resources and supports at the school level are implemented. My school, the Cornerstone Academy for Social Action, is a safe space for LGBTQ children. Our school partnered with PFLAG in 2016 to bring LGBTQ affirming training

[PDF page 25] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses to our students. These trainings were designed to further uplift the self worth of all our students, and create a climate and culture of empathy, compassion, and acceptance of all children. Families with LGBTQ will send them to our school because we have cultivated an affirming and welcoming environment for young people exploring their identities. As a result, in my office, I have had children who have come out to their families and to the community. What experience do you have to demonstrate you are the best person to represent the office you seek? When I was a little kid, my grandmother and my mother raised me in NYC public housing. I grew up with kids of every background, and it changed my life, all of us a short walk away from excellent schools and museums. When I got older, I thought about how things could have been different if I had never met those kids, and if my mom never found a union job. I chose to become a teacher because I wanted every kid in our city to have a chance to grow up the way I did. Ten years ago, I founded a public middle school in the Bronx, the Cornerstone Academy for Social Action, where I served as the principal until the end of 2019. I built this school based on the principles of equity and restorative justice. My goal has been to create an environment that supports the whole child, fostering their emotional wellbeing and unique interests, all while teaching standard subject matter and working to dismantle the school-to-prison pipeline. I know this work could dramatically change historically oppressed communities nationwide if it were given the platform to do so. I’m proud of our work at CASA, but there’s only so much we can do within a single school. After two decades in public education, I am tired of watching our families struggle to live a good life because they can’t get jobs, health care, housing, the dignity and safety they need. I am tired of seeing hedge funds try to buy out our public school system through privatization. I’ve had enough of a generation of politicians who underfunded our schools and cut our social safety net while building more jails, bailing out Wall Street, accepting corporate PAC donations, and spending trillions of dollars on never-ending wars. Our district is more progressive and diverse than ever, but Representative Engel is a leader who represents the past and isn’t doing enough to build urgency and organize a movement to transform our democracy. Along with many issues at the national level, Engel failed to side with the WFP and other members of Congress who endorsed challengers taking on the rogue IDC. Engel said nothing about Jeff Klein working with Republicans to block progressive legislation. We deserve a Democrat who will fight for all of us, a leader who reflects our district’s progressive values. That’s why I’m running for Congress, and why I’m refusing all corporate PAC and lobbyist contributions. We have a chance to build an America where

[PDF page 26] 2020 Congressional Candidate Questionnaire Responses all of us can thrive. We can fight for a Green New Deal, free public college, Medicare for All, lifting up union families, progressive foreign policy, ending mass incarceration and deportation, and fully investing in our public schools. Please detail any specific policy proposals you may have that will affect the LGBT community. My initial legislative priorities are to reverse the dangerous decisions made by the Trump administration, and reinstate and expand protections for LGBT students. This must be done by passing the Equality Act through the Senate, which would drastically expand protections for LGBTQ people. We must support and protect members of the LGBTQ community. The status quo is unacceptable. Because LGBTQ people face systemic inequality and issues related to poverty, it is critical that we pass a Green New Deal, which includes a federal jobs guarantee. The GND would restructure our entire economy and create thousands of quality jobs, as well as job training programs to build up sustainable industries for decades to come.
